science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 4, 2015: A rail-launched Super Strypi rocket carrying 13 baby satellites failed during its debut launch for the US Air Force
science.description: null On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force planned to launch an experimental rocket for small satellites from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii. The launch didn't according to plan . For this mission, the Air Force was testing out the Super Strypi rocket . The rocket used a rail to help with the liftoff. Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control. When it crashed, it destroyed all of the tiny satellites riding aboard the rocket. The cause? Likely a problem with the first stage motor. The mission lost 13 tiny satellites known as cubesats. Cubesats are a popular option for space missions, because they are small and cheap, and they often operate in swarms. After failing to launch this batch of cubesats, the Super Strypi program never recovered from its failure, and the Air Force never tried launching another one. The U.S. Air Force’s rail-launched Super Strypi rocket lifted off from Hawaii about 9:45 p.m. local time on Nov. 3, 2015,, roared toward the sky and failed less than a minute into the long-awaited flight. (Image credit: U.S. Air Force) Why it mattered The Super Strypi rocket was a 21st century take on a 1960s rocket. It was designed to be a modern version of the three-stage Strypi sounding rocket used for for reentry vehicle and anti-missile target tests. Its three stages, powered by Aerojet Rocketdyne solid rocket motors, was designed to reach orbit, rather than suborbital trajectories common to most sounding rockets. The U.S. Air Force hoped Super Strypi would be a new tool for quick-response launches based on national security needs. Altogether, it was designed to launch small payloads of up to 300 kilograms into space for a mere $15 million per mission . The rocket's primary payload was the ORS-4 satellite, short for Operationally Responsive Space 4, which was built for the Air Force by engineers at the University of Hawaii (who nicknamed it HiakaSat). It was designed to capture Earth imagery and monitor the environment over the course of a year. The 12 other payloads on Super Strypi included eight cubesats for NASA's Edison Demonstration of Smallsat Networks mission, and as well as four others for universities that had been added as secondary payloads. Since the Super Strypi failure, neither the Air Force or Space Force has opted to use the rocket for a new mission. The Space Force has turned instead to commercial companies for fast-turnaround launch support. In June of this year, the U.S. Space Force teamed up with Rocket Lab to launch the Victus Haze mission with just 17 hours of notice , a new record to demonstrate short-turnaround launch response.

science.title: Trump declares 'American space superiority for all eternity' in election night proclamation
science.description: null President Trump issued a declaration yesterday (Nov. 3), proclaiming space open to all humanity for exploration, and the right of American citizens to develop and settle the solar system according to United States laws. "The American Declaration of Freedom in Space," describes space as the "province of all humans" and asserts that the United States will lead humanity's expansion into the cosmos. The proclamation reiterates the administration's goals with NASA's Artemis program to return American astronauts to the moon by 2028 and eventually sending astronauts to Mars , but introduces no new funding, programs or policy directives. "Our Nation will lead the way in the exploration, development, use, and settlement of these new frontiers — forging an interplanetary civilization founded on the enduring and inalienable rights of freedom and individual liberty," the document says. Trump invoked America's "frontier spirit," highlighting Apollo 11 astronauts as the first people in history to walk on the moon's surface and robotic rovers exploring Mars as examples of U.S. leadership, and emphasized the country's flourishing commercial space sector helping ensure "American space superiority for all eternity." "The nation that leads in space will shape the future of humanity," the declaration says, and pledges that America will carry the values of faith, freedom and individual liberty into an interplanetary civilization. The proclamation also highlights the success of NASA's Artemis II mission in April, which carried four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon and set a record for the farthest humans have ever traveled from Earth . The follow-up to that mission, Artemis III, is scheduled to launch next summer (2027), and will test rendezvous and docking operations between NASA's Orion spacecraft and the program's two commercial lunar landers in low Earth orbit . Artemis IV will be the program's first lunar landing mission, and is targeted for 2028. A December 2025 executive order from the President reaffirmed the goal of meeting that timeline, as well as the deployment of the initial elements for a permanent lunar outpost by 2030. Trump's declaration yesterday does not establish new NASA programs, allocate additional funding or issue instructions to federal agencies. Its sweeping language, though, does echo some of the principles in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty , which guarantees freedom of exploration while prohibiting national sovereignty claims on other planets.

science.title: NASA's Swift space telescope crashes back to Earth after failed rescue attempt
science.description: null NASA's Swift space telescope has reached the end of its long and winding road. Swift fell uncontrolled to Earth today (Nov. 4), 22 years after it launched but just three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost it to a higher, life-extending orbit. The 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST (1239 GMT) today over northern Sumatra, according to satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell , who cited U.S. Space Force data. The fall likely didn't make much of an impact; NASA officials predicted beforehand that most of the minibus-sized Swift would burn up as it fell, and they put the odds of any of the surviving pieces hurting anyone on Earth at just 1 in 2,100. Swift — officially known as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer — launched to Earth orbit in November 2004 on a two-year mission to study gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most powerful explosions in the universe . "Swift" was not an acronym but rather referred to the spacecraft's observational agility. "Swift needed to detect and locate gamma-ray bursts, communicate their position to other observatories, and then swing its telescopes around to image the burst locations before their afterglows faded out," S. Bradley Cenko, Swift's principal investigator (PI) at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, said in an Oct. 23 statement . "This typically took Swift about a minute to do." Swift didn't just observe GRBs. It also studied a variety of other cosmic bodies and phenomena, from faraway supernova explosions and feeding black holes to asteroids and comets in our own solar system. And it kept doing this long after its warranty expired — for about 20 years after, in fact. The space telescope didn't conduct its final science observation until this past Oct. 20 . (Swift underwent a name change during this stretch: In 2018, it was rechristened the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory after its first PI, who died the previous year.) "Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long," Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA's Astrophysics Division, said in the same Oct. 23 statement. "In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community," he added. science.description: A new and improved toothbrush could help avoid trips to the dentist Westend61/Alamy A toothbrush that generates electricity may more effectively fight harmful bacteria, while removing plaque, than existing products. The toothbrush uses special bristles that produce electricity as they bend, triggering the formation of molecules that damage bacterial membranes. When put to the test, it led to more than twice the reduction of plaque, gum inflammation and bleeding as conventional toothbrushes. “The concept is great,” says Nicholas Jakubovics at Newcastle University, UK, who wasn’t involved in the research. “Basically, the mechanical forces recharge the surface, so it’s really innovative. Anything that even slightly improves the way dental care works could have a benefit, because oral disease is just so widespread.” Read more How regrowing your own teeth could replace dentures and implants Oral diseases, such as tooth decay, affect nearly half the global population . Brushing regularly can help remove plaque, a sticky layer of bacteria that forms on teeth. These bacteria can produce acids that cause cavities and irritate gums, sometimes leading to tooth loss. Advertisement But even thorough brushing can leave behind bacteria deep in plaque or between teeth, allowing colonies to grow back within hours. Researchers have previously developed toothbrushes with antibacterial metal nanoparticles, including silver and zinc, embedded in their bristles , although their long-term effectiveness is uncertain. Others have designed ionic toothbrushes that use electric currents to help loosen plaque , but they are dependent on batteries. These generate electric charges under pressure , prompting Lu’s team to develop toothbrush bristles made from piezoelectric plastic. science.title: Mars isn't dead — recent volcanic activity reveals it's just sleeping
science.description: null Scientists have long suspected that Mars is geologically "dead," but new spacecraft observations suggest the Red Planet's volcanoes are merely sleeping. That means that Olympus Mons , the extinct Martian volcano that at around 16 miles (26 kilometers) above the surrounding Martian plains is the largest mountain in the solar system , may in fact be a slumbering giant. The observations were made with the European Space Agency (ESA) mission ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) as it studied volcanic fissures along the Alba Mons region of the Red Planet. Alba Mons is in the Tharsis region of Mars, the same area that is home to Olympus Mons. While the latter is the tallest volcano in the solar system, at 374 miles (600 km) across, about the size of Arizona, the Alba Mons region is the largest volcano when considering surface area. TGO detected gas containing hydrogen chloride making its way to the surface of Mars through the Alba Mons fissures. The same gas is commonly found escaping from magmatic vents on Earth, with the compound coming from hot magma beneath the surface. Detecting it on Mars is a sign of dormant Martian volcanism. Orbital imagery had previously shown some volcanoes appear to have been active within the last few million years, and seismometers have detected the rumbling of "marsquakes," both implying the Red Planet is volcanically active. However, eruptions and lava flows have been conspicuous by their absence. "Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," team co-leader and scientist at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences, Daniel Mège, said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "The TGO was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack." Evidence of dormant Martian volcanism is rising Mège and colleagues were first alerted to something strange happening on Mars when they noticed spikes of hydrogen chloride during Martian summer and on the northern hemisphere of the Red Planet. That is both a time and place at which hydrogen chloride shouldn't be detected. The gas usually peaks in the northern hemisphere during winter on Mars, disappearing in the summer. This variation is connected to the water and dust cycle on Mars. An exception to the rule occurs over volcanic fissures on the flanks of the Alba Mons volcano, in early summer. The TGO followed up on this by detecting fresh and narrow fissures, in some cases hundreds of feet long, in the Alba Mons region. A clear sign of volcanism. "It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," Mège said. science.title: Tom Gauld on our future robot overlords
A dyslexia diagnosis can help struggling children, but what about the rest?
science.description: Shutterstock/Jakub Krechowicz In years gone by, children who struggled to learn to read and spell were labelled “stupid”, “lazy” or “dim”. Today, of course, we are much more enlightened – now we label many of these children as “dyslexic”. But perhaps this label is still a bad idea. Picture two 9-year-olds reading at the level of an average 6-year-old. One gets a diagnosis of dyslexia. This positively affects her wellbeing. Her teachers now understand she has dyslexia and that she can get tailored help. The other child isn’t so lucky. Maybe his parents can’t afford a dyslexia test – in the UK, assessment isn’t available on the NHS and can cost several hundred pounds. In the US it could set parents back thousands of dollars. Or perhaps he was tested but the result was negative. Until very recently, this outcome was common for already disadvantaged children, because the official definition of dyslexia included the idea of “discrepancy” – that reading problems should be unexpected given a child’s other cognitive abilities. Assessing ability using IQ tests can also be biased against those from lower socioeconomic groups or learning to read in a second language. By extension, this second child is just bad at reading or lazy, or both, and not eligible to receive extra help with reading. Advertisement Two children with the same learning difficulty. One gets help, the other does not Two children with the same learning difficulty. One gets help and understanding and the other doesn’t, all because of a label. Yet this label is based on a questionable assessment. Despite trials using a wide range of cognitive processes, researchers have been unable to find meaningful ways to identify dyslexia. So, why not just help all children who struggle to read? Each has a unique combination of risk and remediation factors, but all will benefit most if we intervene when the problem first shows up, instead of waiting years for them to fail and then receive a diagnosis. Our newfound understanding of what is happening in their brains even suggests some surprisingly simple ways to help . Giving every child the best possible chance to overcome their challenge is what matters, not the label we attach to them.

science.title: The DNA is backwards on The Selfish Gene’s cover – again
science.description: Josie Ford Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more Don’t get it twisted Feedback is not young. We have been here on the back pages for many years, endlessly pushing a boulder up a hill and trying to take joy in the effort. This means, every so often, we are forced to repeat ourselves – because the world repeats itself. With a due sense of ennui, we turn our world-weary eyes to the cover of the new 50th anniversary edition of Richard Dawkins’s popular science classic The Selfish Gene . The title, written in all-caps, takes up most of the cover. The “I” in “SELFISH” has been replaced by a colourful little drawing of a DNA double helix. Advertisement Alas, something is awry. Geneticist Simon Fisher pointed it out on Bluesky : “You know a gene is selfish when its DNA twists the wrong way, as demonstrated by the left-handed double-helix proudly adorning the 50th Anniversary Edition of the multimillion copy bestseller on this topic.” Yes, once again we have an example of a DNA molecule being drawn, essentially, backwards. In reality, it is a right-handed double helix, but the one on the book cover is left-handed. It’s twisting the wrong way. Feedback’s mind’s eye immediately cast itself back to March 2025 , when we covered a Lego model that included many scientific and technological objects, including a sadly left-handed DNA. It turns out that The Selfish Gene ‘s art has been wrong for at least a decade. Patrick Goymer , an editor at PLOS One , shared the cover of the 40th anniversary edition on Bluesky, and it has the same left-handed DNA in place of the “I”. Feedback notes that our own copy is the 30th anniversary edition, and the DNA is correct. At some point since 2006, the DNA on the cover has flipped into a mirror universe. This little mistake would be doubly embarrassing if, say, the Nobel prize in chemistry had recently been awarded for research into these sorts of mirror molecules. Can you imagine? Such is the case with a paper published in Cureus , titled: “Massive fecaloma dissolved by Coca-Cola: A case report”. It was sent to us by Australia reporter Alice Klein, who either has a truly terrible browser history or makes extensive use of a VPN. A faecaloma, for those not yet blessed with the knowledge, is a large lump of impacted faeces trapped in a person’s rectum. In this case report, the faecaloma had a maximum diameter of 12.2 centimetres. Based on our own personal experience, we do not recommend watching this sequence over dinner.
